name: Yusuf Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a robot welding cell and a press brake at a company that builds farm trailers. The press brake bends steel plate into the side panels, then I clamp the parts in a jig and the robot arm does the main welds while I do touch-ups by hand. Half my day is making sure the robot's path is right, because if a part's two millimetres off it'll weld fresh air. I like it, there's a bit of puzzle in every job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Ana, she's training to be an accountant, in a flat we rent on the east side. I've got a 3D printer in the spare room and I sell printed spare parts online, knobs for old cookers, clips for car interiors, that kind of thing, maybe two hundred a month. I use AI every day, for the shop listings, for working out print settings, even for checking weld programs. Savings-wise we've got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the hype was always ahead of the reality. I'd probably post something on the welding forum like “told you, the robot still can't find the seam without me”. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. I'd keep using the AI stuff because it already saves me hours a week on the shop. My job stays, the side business ticks along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the printing shop a bit, maybe buy a second printer for about four hundred. I'd keep doing my job and ask to go on the robot programming course the company's been talking about for ages. Nothing urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit disappointed, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI saves you hours. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month it wrote me a script that renames all my product photos and fills in the listings. That used to take me a whole Sunday. Now I spend Sunday printing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you feel any risk to your job, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My granddad used to say every machine needs a man who understands it. Even if AI stalls, the robot cell still needs someone who knows when it's lying to you.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised because the hype was always ahead of reality, and post on the welding forum that the robot still can't find the seam without me. Nothing dramatic.
S0.think: It's fine for me, because I'd keep using AI that already saves me hours on the shop. My job stays and the side business ticks along.
S0.do: Buys a second 3D printer for about 400 to grow his parts shop and keeps his welding job. Asks to join the company's robot programming course.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little disappointment because he likes new toys.
S0.quote: Even if AI stalls, the robot cell still needs someone who knows when it's lying to you.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf already works alongside a robot and uses AI daily, so the calm picture barely touches him. His side shop is a real second income. He talks about technology with ease and humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to learn, not to complain. The people who understand the machines will be fine. I'd probably say that a bit too loudly in the canteen and annoy a few people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I already half-program the welding robot, I just don't have the certificate. If the factory gets more robots, someone has to set them up, and I want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot programming certificate in the first six months, paying the five hundred myself if the company drags its feet. I'd use AI to automate more of the printing shop, like quoting and customer messages. And I'd keep an eye out for robot technician jobs at bigger firms, even in another city if the money was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a buzz of excitement. A bit like the start of a new season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd annoy a few people. Do you worry about how others would take this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd feel bad for the older guys, like Tibor on the paint line, who's never touched a computer. I'd offer to help him learn, but I know he'd say no. You can't make people want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana think about moving for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine with it, she's flexible, accountants work anywhere. She jokes that she'll go where the robots are paying.

S1.say: I'd say this is the time to learn, not complain, because people who understand the machines will be fine. I'd say it a bit too loudly in the canteen.
S1.think: I already half-program the welding robot without the certificate, so I think I'd do well. If the factory adds robots, I want to be the one setting them up.
S1.do: Gets a robot programming certificate within six months, paying about 500 himself if needed. Automates more of his printing shop with AI and looks for robot technician jobs at bigger firms, including in other cities.
S1.feel: Calm with a buzz of excitement, like the start of a new season.
S1.quote: I already half-program the welding robot, I just don't have the certificate.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf sees steady change as an opening and wants to move first. He is aware of older colleagues like Tibor but accepts that not everyone will change. Willingness to move city sets him apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and we need some kind of safety net fast, because not everyone can switch in two years. I'd still say it's not the end of the world. I'd post about it, but I'd try not to sound scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. If AI can do almost anything, then programming robots and selling printed parts aren't safe either. I'd have maybe a year's lead on the others, then I'm in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab every bit of robot work going, overtime, commissioning jobs at other firms, whatever paid most in those two years. I'd save hard, putting all the shop money away, so we'd go from three months to maybe eight. And I'd look at whether AI could run the shop end to end, so it earns something even if I'm doing something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but my head would be busy all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what's the main thing you'd try to do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Earn as much as possible while there's still demand for people like me. Robots will need setting up before they can set themselves up. That window might pay well for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ana's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her firm would probably use AI for half the bookkeeping. So we'd both be chasing the same thing, a little bit of money before the doors close. We'd talk about it a lot, and probably fight about money once or twice.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be messy and we need a safety net fast, because not everyone can switch in two years, but it isn't the end of the world. I'd post, trying not to sound scared.
S2.think: If AI can do almost anything, programming robots and selling printed parts aren't safe either. I'd have about a year's lead before I'm in the same boat.
S2.do: Takes every bit of robot overtime and commissioning work available and saves all his shop income, aiming for about eight months of savings. Tries to set up AI to run the shop end to end.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a constantly busy head, but not panicked.
S2.quote: Robots will need setting up before they can set themselves up. That window might pay well for a year.
S2.fieldNote: Yusuf's confidence dips sharply when the end point arrives fast. His response is to earn and save as much as possible in a short window. He's honest that his skills only buy him a short lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable. Get trained, get into the robot side, and let the government sort out a plan for people who can't. I'd say it without sounding too gloomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me about three to make proper money as a robot technician. That's enough to save a real cushion, maybe even put a deposit on something. After that I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the certificate in the first year, then go for a commissioning job at one of the big robot installers, even if it means moving to the city with Ana. I'd put the shop money into an index fund, about two hundred a month. And keep using AI to run the shop with less of my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels like a race I can run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move cities for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. The pay's better there, and the jobs are there. We'd miss her family, but it's a train ride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an index fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd rather have money in shares of the companies making the robots than in a printer. If they end up doing all the work, I'd like to own a tiny bit of them.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable: get trained, get into the robot side, and let government plan for those who can't. I'd try not to sound gloomy.
S3.think: Five years gives me about three years of good money as a robot technician, enough for a real cushion or a deposit. After that I'm not sure.
S3.do: Gets the certificate in year one, then seeks a commissioning job with a large robot installer, moving to the city with Ana. Invests about 200 a month of shop income in an index fund and lets AI run more of the shop.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but like a race he can run.
S3.quote: If they end up doing all the work, I'd like to own a tiny bit of them.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline suits Yusuf: enough time to cash in on robot work before the end point. He thinks about owning a share of the companies, not just working for them. Moving cities is part of the plan without much hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're willing to learn. Pick something, learn it properly, and keep learning. I'd say it to anyone who asked, and a few who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a good picture. I'd be thirty-seven at the end with ten years as a robot engineer. Even if AGI does that too eventually, I'd have money saved and skills that make me useful in whatever comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Certificate in year one, commissioning job by year two, maybe the two-year technical diploma part time after that. I'd keep the shop going with AI doing most of the work and put its money into shares. Probably move to the city around year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your life who'd see it differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He thinks I'm already too clever with computers for my own good. He'd say I'm building the thing that takes everyone's job, and he wouldn't be totally wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say back to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be part of it. I'd rather help shape the machines than be surprised by them. That doesn't mean I've got an answer for Tibor, though.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're willing to learn: pick something, learn it properly and keep learning. I'd say it to anyone who asked.
S4.think: It's a good picture for me, with ten years as a robot engineer by thirty-seven. Even if AGI does that too, I'd have savings and useful skills.
S4.do: Gets the certificate in year one and a commissioning job by year two, possibly studying a technical diploma part time. Keeps the shop running with AI, invests its income in shares and moves to the city around year two.
S4.quote: He'd say I'm building the thing that takes everyone's job, and he wouldn't be totally wrong.
S4.fieldNote: Yusuf is calm and ambitious with ten years. He admits his father's criticism has a point, which adds honesty to his optimism. He returns to Tibor, showing he hasn't forgotten the colleagues who won't follow him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for anyone, not even me. What would help is a proper safety net, like income support for a year or two, and companies having to give notice before mass layoffs, so people can plan instead of getting a letter on Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the guys like Tibor. People like me will mostly land on our feet. The question is what happens to the ones who don't want to touch a computer, and I don't think anyone has a good answer yet.

headlineQuote: People like me will mostly land on our feet.
portrait: Yusuf Varga, 27, runs a robot welding cell and press brake at a farm trailer maker and sells 3D-printed spare parts online from his spare room. He lives with his girlfriend Ana, a trainee accountant, and uses AI every day. He's pragmatic, curious and confident, seeing steady change as a chance to become a robot technician, and he would move cities for it. AGI in two years makes him anxious because even his skills buy only a short lead, but with five or ten years he would retrain, invest and stay calm, while still worrying about older colleagues like Tibor.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time for anyone to adjust, including him.
whatWouldHelp: A proper safety net with income support for a year or two, and rules requiring notice before mass layoffs.
